results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** Countable Choice; the spin label $s$; a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $V$; a differentiable unitary representation $D$ with the single spin-$s$ generator block; and the standard cover $\rho:SU(2)\to SO(3)$.

[A1] Countable Choice (AC$_\omega$) is the choice-function principle for every countable family of nonempty sets. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The finite spin-block theorem decomposes the self-adjoint triple into an orthogonal sum of nonzero invariant spin blocks. Under this item's irreducibility hypothesis there can be only one block: any block is invariant under all three $J_i$, so two or more blocks would give a nonzero proper invariant subspace. The single block has highest weight equal to the largest $J_z$ eigenvalue $s$ and an orthonormal basis $v_k$, $k=0,\ldots,2s$, with $J_zv_k=(s-k)v_k$ and the stated finite spin ladder coefficients. [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-block-decomposition]]

[F2] Under AC$_\omega$, $\rho:SU(2)\to SO(3)$ is a surjective two-sheeted covering homomorphism with kernel $\{I,-I\}$. [[ex-su-two-to-so-three-as-a-covering-homomorphism]]

[F3] A unitary representation is a homomorphism into bijective complex-linear isometries, and unitary equivalence means there is a unitary intertwiner. [[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]]

[F4] The scalar complex exponential is the everywhere-convergent power series $\exp z=\sum_{k=0}^\infty z^k/k!$, also written $e^z$. [[def-complex-exponential]]

[F5] $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$ for all $z,w\in\mathbb C$. [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]

[F6] $\exp$ is entire with $\exp'(z)=\exp z$. [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]

[F7] For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$, $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$, and $\exp(i\pi)=-1$. [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]

[F8] For every real $x$, $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]

[F9] Sine and cosine are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with derivatives cosine and minus sine. [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]

[F10] For real $x,y$, $\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y$ and $\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y$. [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]]

[F11] For differentiable real scalar functions on a real interval, sums and scalar multiples differentiate termwise, and $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$. [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]

[F12] A real function continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ satisfies $f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)$ for some $c\in(a,b)$. [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]



1.1 We use real-parameter differentiation in the finite orthonormal basis supplied by [F1]. For a complex scalar $f=a+ib$ with real components, its derivative is $a'+ib'$: convergence of the complex difference quotient is equivalent to convergence of its two real coordinates, since $|x|,|y|\le|x+iy|\le|x|+|y|$. Expanding $(a+ib)(c+id)=(ac-bd)+i(ad+bc)$ transfers [F11] to complex scalar products, and conjugation differentiates by conjugating the derivative. Finite sums then give the scalar-vector and matrix product rules entry by entry, and $(M^*)'=(M')^*$. These entry derivatives are the finite-dimensional vector or operator derivatives: in an orthonormal basis the squared vector norm is the finite sum of squared coordinate moduli, while for a $d\times d$ matrix $A$, each coordinate of $Ax$ has modulus at most $d\max_{j,k}|A_{jk}|\,\|x\|$ by the finite triangle inequality and $|x_k|\le\|x\|$. Thus $\|Ax\|^2\le d^3(\max_{j,k}|A_{jk}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus entrywise difference-quotient remainders tending to zero also tend to zero in the corresponding norm. Direct calculation for each displayed Pauli matrix gives $\sigma_i^*=\sigma_i$, $\sigma_i^2=I$, $\operatorname{tr}\sigma_i=0$, and $\det\sigma_i=-1$. With $c=\cos(t/2)$ and $s_t=\sin(t/2)$, direct $2\times2$ matrix calculations and the Pythagorean identity [F8] give $A_i(t)^*A_i(t)=(c^2+s_t^2)I=I$ and $\det A_i(t)=c^2+s_t^2=1$, so each $A_i(t)$ lies in $SU(2)$. Its entries are differentiable by [F9]. The addition formulas [F10] and $\sigma_i^2=I$ give $A_i(t+h)=A_i(t)A_i(h)$ for each $i$, and [F9] gives $A_i(0)=I$; thus each map $t\mapsto A_i(t)$ is a homomorphism from $(\mathbb R,+)$ to $SU(2)$. Differentiating $D(A_i(t))^*D(A_i(t))=I$ at $0$ and using $\frac{d}{dt}D(A_i(t))|_{t=0}=-iJ_i$ gives $J_i^*=J_i$. For $i=z$, the Euler formula [F7] and parity [F8] give $A_z(t)=\operatorname{diag}(\exp(-it/2),\exp(it/2))$. Set $U(t):=D(A_z(t))$. Since $D$ is a differentiable representation, $U$ is differentiable, $U(t+h)=U(t)U(h)=U(h)U(t)$, and the generator convention gives $U'(0)=-iJ_z$. Differentiating the two products with respect to $h$ at $0$ yields $U'(t)=U(t)(-iJ_z)=(-iJ_z)U(t)$. [F1, F3, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], the irreducibility hypothesis leaves one spin-$s$ block, with orthonormal basis $v_k$, $k=0,\ldots,2s$, and $J_zv_k=(s-k)v_k$. Write $\mu_k=s-k$ and $u_k(t)=U(t)v_k$. Step 1.1 gives $u_k'(t)=-i\mu_k u_k(t)$. From [F5] and [F6], the scalar map $t\mapsto\exp(i\mu_k t)$ has derivative $i\mu_k\exp(i\mu_k t)$: its difference quotient at $t$ factors as $\exp(i\mu_k t)(\exp(i\mu_k h)-1)/h$ and the second factor tends to $i\mu_k$. The coordinate product rule established in step 1.1 gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\exp(i\mu_k t)u_k(t))=0$. To justify constancy, write this vector in the fixed finite orthonormal basis of [F1]. Every real and imaginary coordinate has zero derivative on $\mathbb R$ and is continuous (its increment is its difference quotient times the real increment). For arbitrary $a<b$, apply [F12] separately to these real coordinate functions on $[a,b]$; each has equal endpoint values. All coordinates, and hence the vector, are therefore constant on $\mathbb R$ and equal $v_k$ at $t=0$. Consequently $U(t)v_k=\exp(-i\mu_k t)v_k$. [F1, F5, F6, F11, F12, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $N=2s\in\mathbb N_0$. For every $k=0,\ldots,2s$, $2(s-k)=N-2k$ is an integer and [F5], [F7] give $\exp(-i2\pi(s-k))=\exp(-i\pi N)\exp(i2\pi k)=(-1)^N$. Indeed, $\exp(-i\pi)=-1$ follows from $\exp(i\pi)=-1$ and $\exp(-i\pi)\exp(i\pi)=\exp(0)=1$; also $\exp(i2\pi)=\exp(i\pi)^2=1$. Repeated use of [F5] gives the displayed integer powers. Thus step 2.1 implies $U(2\pi)v_k=(-1)^{2s}v_k$ for every basis vector. [F5, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By the diagonal form in step 1.1 and [F7], $A_z(2\pi)=\operatorname{diag}(\exp(-i\pi),\exp(i\pi))=-I$. Hence $D(-I)=U(2\pi)$; step 3.1 evaluates this operator on an orthonormal basis and proves $D(-I)=(-1)^{2s}I_V$. [F7, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By [F2], every $R\in SO(3)$ has exactly two lifts $W$ and $-W$. The representation law gives $D(-W)=D(-I)D(W)=(-1)^{2s}D(W)$ by step 4.1. The scalar has modulus one by [F7], so the projective class $[D(W)]\in PU(V)$ is independent of the lift. If $R_1=\rho(W_1)$ and $R_2=\rho(W_2)$, then $W_1W_2$ lifts $R_1R_2$, and $[D(W_1W_2)]=[D(W_1)][D(W_2)]$; hence the ray map is a homomorphism. The map is continuous: on any evenly covered neighborhood for $\rho$, its local section $s$ is continuous and the descended map there is $q\circ D\circ s$, a composition of continuous maps. [A1, F2, F3, F7, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 If $s$ is integer, $(-1)^{2s}=1$, so $D(W)$ is independent of the lift; defining $\widetilde D(R)=D(W)$ gives a unitary representation because products of lifts lift the product, as in step 5.1, and it is continuous by the same local-section argument. If $s$ is half-integer, $(-1)^{2s}=-1$, so the two lifts $I$ and $-I$ of the identity have images $I_V$ and $-I_V$; these differ since $V\ne\{0\}$. Therefore $D$ cannot factor as a unitary representation through $\rho$, although its projective class from step 5.1 does factor. [A1, F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and a smooth map between the stated oriented closed surfaces.

[A1] Axiom of Choice is the principle in [[def-axiom-of-choice]], assumed by the top-form pairing supplier.

[A2] Countable Choice is the assumption in [[def-countable-choice]] and in the de Rham isomorphism [[thm-de-rham-theorem]].

[F1] [[def-degree-of-a-map-between-oriented-closed-manifolds]] defines $\deg(n)$ by the induced map on integral fundamental classes.

[F2] [[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]] supplies the orientation classes on both closed surfaces.

[F3] [[thm-de-rham-theorem]] makes the de Rham-to-singular-cohomology comparison natural for smooth maps.

[F4] [[def-kronecker-evaluation-pairing]] and [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]] define its natural evaluation on homology classes.

[F5] [[lem-de-rham-top-integral-is-fundamental-class-evaluation]] identifies integration of a top form with evaluation of its de Rham class on the real fundamental class.

[F6] [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]] defines finite singular chains with coefficients and their boundaries; [[def-induced-singular-chain-map]] sends a simplex to its postcomposition; [[prop-singular-chains-and-homology-are-covariantly-functorial]] gives the induced map on homology.

[F7] Local real-chain evaluation used here: for a space $X$, $C_n(X;\mathbb R)$ is the real vector space of finite formal sums of singular $n$-simplices with the real-linear singular boundary $\partial$. The identification in [[def-singular-cochain-complex-with-coefficients]] gives $C^n(X;\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_n(X;\mathbb R),\mathbb R)$. For a real cocycle $\varphi$ and real cycle $c$, define $\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle_{\mathbb R}:=\varphi(c)$. This is the real-bilinear extension mentioned in [[def-kronecker-evaluation-pairing]]; the cochain pullback representative is given by [[prop-singular-cohomology-is-contravariantly-functorial]], and the pairing's descent and naturality are proved in step 1.1 below.



**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1]–[F7], and $n$ as in the statement.

1.1 If $\varphi'=\varphi+\delta\psi$ is a second representative of the same real cohomology class and $c'=c+\partial b$ a second representative of the same real homology class, then $\varphi'(c')=\varphi(c)+\varphi(\partial b)+(\delta\psi)(c)+(\delta\psi)(\partial b)=\varphi(c)$: the three additional terms vanish respectively by $\delta\varphi=0$, $\partial c=0$, and $\partial^2=0$. Thus the real evaluation in [F7] is independent of representatives. For every continuous $f:X\to Y$, the chain-level formulas $f^*\varphi=\varphi\circ f_\#$ and $f_*c=f_\#c$ give $(f^*\varphi)(c)=\varphi(f_\#c)$, so $\langle f^*[\varphi],[c]\rangle_{\mathbb R}=\langle[\varphi],f_*[c]\rangle_{\mathbb R}$. Linearity of $\varphi$ and $c$ makes the pairing real-bilinear. [F6, F7, algebra]

1.2 In spherical coordinates $x=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$, $z=\cos\theta$, the unnormalized displayed two-form is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Integrating for $0\le\theta\le\pi$ and $0\le\phi\le2\pi$ gives $4\pi$, so $\omega_{S^2}$ is a smooth closed form with integral one; its displayed ambient expression shows it extends smoothly across the coordinate poles. [given, algebra]

2.1 Let $J$ be the natural comparison in [F3]. By [F5] and the real evaluation defined in [F7], $\int_{\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\langle J([n^*\omega_{S^2}]),[\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}]_{\mathbb R}\rangle_{\mathbb R}$. Naturality of $J$ and the real-chain pairing proved in step 1.1 gives $\int_{\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\langle J([\omega_{S^2}]),n_*[\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}]_{\mathbb R}\rangle_{\mathbb R}$. [A1, A2, F3, F5, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], $n_*[\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}]_{\mathbb Z}=\deg(n)[S^2]_{\mathbb Z}$. The coefficient map $\iota:C_\bullet(X;\mathbb Z)\to C_\bullet(X;\mathbb R)$ sends each finite sum $\sum_j a_j\sigma_j$ to $\sum_j a_j\sigma_j$ with the same coefficients viewed in $\mathbb R$. It commutes with boundaries because [F6] defines the singular boundary as an integer linear combination of faces and $\iota$ is additive; it commutes with $n_\#$ because [F6] postcomposes each simplex without changing its coefficient. Hence it induces a coefficient-change map on homology and carries each integral fundamental class to its real fundamental class: it sends the positive local orientation generator $1$ to $1$, so uniqueness of the class with those local restrictions in [F2] identifies the image. Applying $\iota$ to the degree equation gives $n_*[\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}]_{\mathbb R}=\deg(n)[S^2]_{\mathbb R}$. By the real bilinearity in [F7] and steps 2.1, $\int_{\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\deg(n)\langle J([\omega_{S^2}]),[S^2]_{\mathbb R}\rangle_{\mathbb R}=\deg(n)\int_{S^2}\omega_{S^2}=\deg(n)$ by [F5] and step 1.2. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
